text.1_, 21_Siman, 0_Seif Katan: On new vessels. However, one does not recite the Shehecheyanu blessing on the mitzvah, since it does not occur from time to time. Nevertheless, this requires further examination, as in Yoreh De'ah section 28, it is written in the gloss that one recites Shehecheyanu on covering [blood], and in section 265, paragraph 7, it states that one recites Shehecheyanu for circumcision and the redemption of the firstborn. It must be said that those cases are not as common. See Siftei Kohen (Shakh), who wrote something similar to this. However, there is a difficulty, for on new vessels one must recite the blessing at the time of acquisition, as stated in Orach Chaim section 223, paragraph 4. So why does it say [that one recites the blessing] when one makes tzitzit on it? It must be that the case discussed is one where the blessing was not recited at the time of acquisition. Alternatively, the distinction is that one only recites Shehecheyanu when purchasing a garment that is immediately ready to wear. But if one buys fabric and makes it into clothing, then the blessing is recited at the time of wearing, as stated in Orach Chaim section 600, paragraph 2. Here, since one is making tzitzit on it, the blessing is recited incidentally at the time of performing the mitzvah.
text.1_, 80_Siman, 0_Seif Katan: From this language we learn that even if he cannot eat, for example he has a weak constitution, still since others his age can eat, we need to distance ourselves (from the extriment to read shema). This requires analysis as we have not found this in any posek, and in addition the gemara indicates that if he was older, even though he cannot eat a kazayit in the alloted time of a Peras, we still need to distance ourselves from his excrement. This implies that for a child if he cannot eat it then it would be permissible (to say shema). Therefore it appears to me that the law is that if someone his age can eat, the assumption is he can also. And if we know that he cannot because he is weak etc, even if he is 3 or 4 years old we don't need to distance ourselves. And if he was an adult, even if he cannot eat, we still need to distance ourselves.  The Bach adds that we also don't distance ourselves from (extrement) of a minor if we know that that specific extrement did not come from grain, for example he hasn't eaten grain for days like Rashi writes. The poskim write like this. And if we know he has never eaten grain, even if he is a few years old, you don't need to distance. Rashi writes that all 5 grains are called dagan and the feces smells. In yoreh death 265:8 it seems that it is better to distance oneself from extrement, even of a minor, even if he is 8 days. The Maharshal says it is not proper to read Shema next to a baby as it is probably dirty from garbage. End of his words. It seems to me for a different reason, that they don't clean themselves properly, and feces around the anus, even though it is covered is forbidden (to read by it). Look at siman 76:6
text.1_, 101_Siman, 4_Seif Katan: But on their sides.  And in the Zohar Chayei Sarah page 313 it say that on any side is prohibited.
text.1_, 122_Siman, 5_Seif Katan: 6. On days that they say piyutim (before the chazans repetition) on should take (3 steps) forward when the chazan begins his repetition (Lechem Chamudos). The Kesef Mishna writes (9:4) if one wants he can just continue standing where he ended up (after taking the steps back) and not take steps forward. However according to the one explanation of the three steps brought in the Beis Yosef you really need 6 steps (and we include the steps you take forward). Therefore according to this opinion one must take three steps forwards. For this reason were careful not to have people pass infront of others when there standing in there place (after taking three steps back) to not interrupt between the six steps (Lechem Chamudos). See siman 95 sif 1 (where the Rama brings an opinion that need to take three steps forward before Shemoneh eshrei aswell. If so you already have 6 steps, 3 before shemona esrie and 3 after). And also see siman 124 (sif 1 brings from the kesavim to take 3 steps forward at kedusha and wait there until tachanun) and siman 131 sif 2 (where he says if one doesn't have a seat where he took 3 steps to then should take the steps back to get to his seat to sit).
text.1_, 123_Siman, 3_Seif Katan: 4.The explanation of this phrase is that you won't finish all 18 berachot of shemoneh eshrei within the time your allowed to daven in (Lechem Chamudot). And he (the Rama) also writes this in siman 232 at the end of sif 1 (if not enough time chazan should begin repetition immediately).
text.1_, 130_Siman, 14_Seif Katan: "On Tu B'Av" - Many reasons are brought in Bava Batra 121, that [this day] was a great Yom Tov (holiday)  during the time of the Temple.
text.1_, 130_Siman, 15_Seif Katan: "On Tu Bishvat" - The New Year (Rosh Hashanah) for for the trees. And the Ashkenazim customarily [eat] many types of fruits from trees. (Tikkun Ysoscher 62:25)
text.1_, 138_Siman, 12_Seif Katan: “…He has to hold…” In (Sefer) Kavanot it is written that before the blessing he shall hold the two handles (of the scroll) and during the blessing he shall take away his left hand to give strength to his right hand. And in these manuscripts (?), it is written that during the blessing he shall hold with his two hands the writing sheets of the Torah through the wrapping (around the scroll) and after the blessing he shall remove the left (hand).
text.1_, 165_Siman, 0_Seif Katan: Either way, one is not allowed to pour hot water into the wine since one is focused on being precise and that would be too much of a loss of focus (tosfot 106b, and Bach). This law applies to anything similar to this.  It is also written there in the name of Rabeinu Tam that it is forbidden to do these on a week day as one my lose focus and leave to do other things, but on the Shabbat when the table is all set, one can wash hands and then make kiddush. The same law applies to making havdala and then eating. See what is written in siman 174
text.1_, 165_Siman, 1_Seif Katan: The Shela writes that each day, before washing for bread, a person should give a prayer for the food he receives from G-d, and if he forgot to say this prayer until after he washed he is allowed to say it before saying the beracha on bread. And the world has a custom to say tehillim 23 between washing and hamotzi (see Siman 235:2 - where the Rema says that one doesn't break within the meal but one does break before hamotzi to say Shema and other prayers that were missed).  The Rashal writes that the host should let the greatest man wash last (to allow him to talk until the end/or to not cause him to pause for too long..), but if he was asked first to wash and he chooses to wait till later, this is a transgressions since he is causing others to have a break, rather he should wash and sit down and not speak, and if they ask him a dvar tora he is permitted to stop. End of words of Rashal. See Sman 167:5 (where the SA lists thing that should be at the table in preparation for the beracha). And the Bach writes that it is forbidden to speak, even with divrei Torah, and even the sitting down is a hefsek as the Rema writes (ie, waiting more than 22 amot). With this in mind, a great man can choose not to wash first since we are more concerned when the person saying the beracha has to wait, as opposed to those that are listening. If the guests see that it is taking too long, they can take a piece of bread and recite the blessings for themselves
text.1_, 165_Siman, 2_Seif Katan: The tosfot in Sota prove this point from the case of a Metzora. A metzora was not able to do semicha on the sacrifice immediately before the slaughter as they were not allowed to enter the Azara. What they did was do semicha outside the entrance gates (Nikanor gates) and then the kohanim to walk the animal to the Mizbeach for the sacrifice. The distance between the gate and the alter is 22 amot and we see it was not a hefsek (the semicha needs to be just before the sacrifice). But I have a problem. This braita is brought in zevachim 33a to argue prove that a small amount that enters is not considered entering until the entire person enters (otherwise, why doesn't the metzora put his hand inside for smicha and then do shchita right there at the entrance). This question is origonally based on the assumption that we are talking about chachamim that you can shecht anywhere in the Azara, and then concludes that it is according to R Yehuda that only by the mizbeach is fine.  But I have an issue, let us just say...... (not sure), rather we must conclude that if you move from one place to another (ie the 22 amot) it should be a hefsek. Even small amount of walking. That is how the mishne in Middot (end of ch2)  seems to imply that in the place of smicha you need shchita. This needs analysis. (Look at siman 8,13 where the SA says that if you make a blessing in your home on tzitzit and then walk to shul you need another blessing for tallis as the walk is a hefsek. Look also at Siman 181:6 about waiting after mayim achronim). And it requires analysis on what it says in Yora Deah 19 where the psak is (if the slaughter house is messy) to say a bracha outside of the slaughterhouse at a distance of 4 Amon as it needs to be in its place (even bracha achrona 184 needs to be in its place. All the more so the first bracha. I looked at the Aguda in chulin (where it says 4 amot) and the 4 amot seem to be in the same house. This is what is mentioned in Shabbos "someone who wants to drink in the washhouse, should bless in the outside room since it is like a corner to a corner". But according to tosfot even corner to corner would be a hefsek and this is the prevailing opinion since it is no less that speaking. Therefore the position of the Rema in Yore Dea needs further analysis.
text.1_, 166_Siman, 1_Seif Katan: Bless "Hamotzi lechem min ha'aretz" [Who takes out bread from the ground] - (And if many people are eating together, the people dining should direct their heart (intention) to the person saying the beracha, and answer amen, and the person saying the beracha should give intention to the amen - Or Zarua). And one pauses slightly between the word "lechem" [bread] and the word "min" [from].
text.1_, 166_Siman, 2_Seif Katan: Do not bless "Hamotzi" before grasping the bread.
text.1_, 166_Siman, 3_Seif Katan: Put both hands on the bread when you are about to bless "Hamotzi"; for the 10 fingers are reflective of the 10 mitzvot that are dependent on bread. Additionally, there are 10 words in the blessing of "Hamotzi" and 10 words in the following verses: Psalms 104:14, "He causes the grass to grow for the cattle, and grass for the service of man: that he may bring forth bread out of the land." Psalms 145:15, "The eyes of all look to you expectantly, and you give them their food at the proper time." Deuteronomy 8:8, "A land of wheat and barley, of vines, figs, and pomegranates, a land of olive trees and honey." Bresheit 27:28, "May G!d give you from the dew of heaven and fat of the earth, and an abundance of grain and wine."
text.1_, 166_Siman, 13_Seif Katan: The Beis Yosef writes in the name of Tosafos [who] quotes the Medrash, that when the Jewish people are sitting and waiting (after washing) for each other before making Hamotzie, and they are without any mitzvos, The Satan stands to prosecute them. The covenant of salt protects them. Also see Siman 166 [where it states] that it is better to talk words of Torah that to sit idle. and better than both is to avoid an interruption altogether.
text.1_, 172_Siman, 0_Seif Katan: The laws of meat and milk are explained in Yoreh De’ah, for that is their place, but I saw that the Bach wrote here as follows: "it implies that when they do not recognize one another they may eat on one tablecloth, and he wondered, etc., that perhaps meat and cheese might stick together on the tablecloth, etc., and it seems to me that here it speaks of a new tablecloth or one that was well laundered, and this one eats at one end and that one eats at the other end, so that they do not touch each other, and it is obvious; furthermore he wrote that when one places a meat bowl on the table and afterward places a dairy pot in its place it absorbs the taste of the meat absorbed in the table, etc., and forbids to the extent of a peel’s thickness" but we do not hold this way as written in Yoreh De’ah at the end of siman 92 that absorption does not transfer from vessel to vessel; and there are those who have the custom to wash between cheese and fish, and this came from what the Beit Yosef wrote in Yoreh De’ah siman 87 that it is dangerous to eat cheese and fish, but it was already written in the Darkei Moshe that there is a scribal error there in the Beit Yosef and it should read fish with meat, see there, and so wrote the later authorities: For it is difficult according to another view, and it is possible that nowadays there is not so much danger, for we see many things mentioned in the Gemara as dangerous because of evil spirit and other matters that nowadays are not harmful because the natures have changed, and everything depends on the nature of the lands, and see Yoreh De’ah 116:3 and Even HaEzer 156, and so wrote the Bach in the name of the Rambam.
text.1_, 176_Siman, 6_Seif Katan: That we do not, etc." It is written in Levush that during large meals, people would refrain from eating bread, and even though pieces of bread were left on the table, they did not intend to eat them. This also appears to be the implication in the Tur. However, the Bach wrote that our custom follows the Tosafot, which state that we always intend to eat the bread. Nevertheless, it seems to me (Le'aniyut Da'ati) that the reason is as written in Tosafot Rid, who states: "Specifically in their days, when it was customary to remove the tables before Birkat HaMazon, it appeared as a separate meal. But for us, since we do not remove the table, even if we have finished eating, as long as we have not recited the blessing, it is still considered part of the meal
text.1_, 224_Siman, 3_Seif Katan: A Bar Mitzvah - It happens when a boy becomes 13 years and one day old. Now it is customary to bless when the young man leads prayers or reads Torah on shabbat for the first time, because then it is known publicly that he is bar mitzvah (Lechem Hamudot). Yalkut Hadash says that a person is commanded to make a feast on the day his son becomes a bar mitzvah, like the day he gets married. It is obvious that it happens when a boy enters his 14th year. In Yam Shel Shlomo, chapter 7 of Bava Kamma it says that if the young man gives a dvar torah it is a seudat mitzvah even if it doesn't happen on the day [that he turns 13 and one day].
text.1_, 224_Siman, 4_Seif Katan: From this punishment - The explanation is that until now the father was punished when the son sinned because he did not educate his son. The Levush explains the opposite - until now the son was punished for the father's sins. See there.
text.1_, 228_Siman, 0_Seif Katan: "Faithful"--and those who say "faithful, etc.," before the blessing, they are making a mistake
text.1_, 228_Siman, 1_Seif Katan: "And it is forbidden to look"--And one who looks at it in excess, his eyes are darkness
text.1_, 229_Siman, 5_Seif Katan: Not only bloodletting, but anything to do with healing is a cause for this blessing. And one who sneezes, and his friend says "Assuta!" (healing!), s/he should respond 'Blessed be you', and then say 'I hope for Your salvation, God' . For one who prays for another is answered first.
text.1_, 262_Siman, 11_Seif Katan: She blesses after lighting, because if she blesses it becomes an acceptance of Shabbat and it would be forbidden to light. Therefore on Yom Tov, she should bless and then light - this was written in the [introduction to the] Drisha in the name of his mother. But woman have no intelligence, etc. Our sages made no distinction between these cases, as we see in siman 158, see there, and the Tosafot in Pesachim 7b.
text.1_, 262_Siman, 12_Seif Katan: And to make a blessing on it. Because lighting [Shabbat] candles is obligatory, for the sake of peace at home (shalom bayit), that one not trip over wood or stone (Mordechai). And even those who say that the candle of Yom Kippur does not require a blessing, in any case, here it is used for the necessities of eating—preparing their utensils and dishes, which is not the case on Yom Kippur. And all the more so for us, who believe that one does make a blessing on Yom Kippur, because we think that shalom bayit applies even without eating (Mahari”l, Responsa, No. [144] 155).
text.1_, 306_Siman, 30_Seif Katan: 31. "It is forbidden to hint." And so similarly it is prohibited to say something such that he [the idolater non-Jew] will thereby understand that he should perform a prohibited act. (Rakna"t Section 99) And thus it is prohibited to tell the idolater non-Jew "wipe your nose" such that he thereby understand that he should remove the soot from the head of the lamp, for specifically to say to him something by which he will understand that he should perform the act after Shabbat is permitted as written in subsection 7. But if the non-Jew does it on Shabbat, it is prohibited -- for even if the non-Jew performs labor on his own for the sake of  a Jew, it is prohibited to benefit from it (the labor), as is written in Section 325; all the more so to hint to him, as against the Bach (look there), and look at what is written in subsection 14 in the name of Rm"m, for there we don't prohibit it because it was asked of an idolater non-Jew but rather that he told him that he can't read it.
text.1_, 307_Siman, 40_Seif Katan: 41. THERE ARE THOSE WHO SAY THAT THE LAW OF STONES, ETC. This is what the Mordechai wrote, that there is no difference and to the contrary, he wrote there that there are those who say specifically regarding branches there is a disagreement. But stones are different because they do not move. And we heard a little bit about this in the R"an ספי"ז. Therefore we can say the opinion of the Rosh on all of this, ועמ"ש סי' שכ"ה סי"א וצ"ע, how can you say there is no disagreement regarding stones? There is a disagreement specifically in the Gemara Shabbos 125! Therefore it seems to be that certainly because they (stones) do not move, certainly it is permitted to sit on them because according to everyone, it is not forbidden to touch Muktze.
text.1_, 307_Siman, 41_Seif Katan: 42. Because if this happens, he performed an action.
text.1_, 317_Siman, 1_Seif Katan: Motzai Shabbos immediately. For specifically when a gentile is doing it do we require 'bichdei sheyase' for we suspect he might instruct him to do so [again] whereas [even if he were to instruct a Jew to transgress shabbos for him] the Jew would never listen.
text.1_, 327_Siman, 5_Seif Katan: If the patient does not want the medicine, we force the patient to take it. If the patient says he requires a certain medicine, and the doctor says the patient does not need it, we listen to the patient. If [however] the doctor says that that medicine will harm [the patient], we listen to the doctor. (Radvaz 1 6 25)
text.1_, 425_Siman, 0_Seif Katan: Women are patur: because it is a mitzvah aseh shehazman grama. And even though they fulfill all the mitzvot aseh like Sukkah, nonetheless they do not fulfill this one, because they caused the moon to wane (Shelah) see what he wrote at the end of #296. And in Sanhedrin ch. 5 it says regarding blessing the moon “our women also make this blessing”, somewhat implying that they make the blessing, but possibly this is a figure of speech.
text.1_, 427_Siman, 0_Seif Katan: The general principle: one must always ensure that Yom Kippur does not fall on Sunday or Friday, so that there won't be two holy days adjacent to each other, and also that Hoshanah Rabbah should not fall on Shabbat, which would cause the willow ritual to be postponed. "And on the day that Shavuot falls, Chanukah will be...": This should be explained as follows: on the day that Shavuot falls, the following Chanukah will be either regular or deficient in days. But when the months are full, it will fall on the day after Shavuot. For example, if Shavuot is on Sunday, Chanukah will be on Monday.
text.1_, 427_Siman, 2_Seif Katan: "MBHC is a leap year": Meaning when Rosh Hashanah falls on Thursday and the year is a leap year, then Parashat Noah is read on Rosh Chodesh Cheshvan and one additional Shabbat is inserted.
text.1_, 427_Siman, 3_Seif Katan: "Bamidbar Sinai before Shavuot": Because Shavuot is Rosh Hashanah for trees, therefore we read one section after the rebukes so that the year and its curses should conclude. For this reason we read Atem Nitzavim before Rosh Hashanah.
text.1_, 427_Siman, 4_Seif Katan: "HaMelech": This refers to Rosh Hashanah when we say "HaMelech HaMishpat." "Pat VaYelech": This means dividing into pieces—that Nitzavim and VaYelech are split into two readings.
text.1_, 427_Siman, 5_Seif Katan: "Paqdo and Pascho": Paqdo is imperative form, meaning we are commanded to read close to Pesach. Sagro—the language of a quarantined leper. Meno—Bamidbar Sinai where Israel was counted. Tzomo—Tisha B'Av. Tzalo—VaEtchanan. Qomo—Atem Nitzavim. When Pesach falls on Shabbat, the Jews in Israel read Shemini on the following Shabbat; some separate Tazria and Metzora, some separate Behar and Bechukotai, and in a leap year they separate Matot and Masei.
text.1_, 427_Siman, 6_Seif Katan: "They divide": In some places they follow Rashi's divisions. I found written that even when there are obligations, the parasha should not be divided further.
text.1_, 427_Siman, 7_Seif Katan: "In the verses before them": Three verses before (according to Beit Yosef and Tosafot). See section 138. In Siman 90 section 56 he struggled to justify our custom of beginning with the curses in Torat Kohanim without starting from the verse before them. Nevertheless, it seems one should begin three verses before. The custom spread because they call the Rav (head of the Beit Din) for the third aliyah every Shabbat, requiring them to read with him up to the rebuke, therefore they begin with the rebuke. But it's preferable that the Rav waive his honor and accept the fourth aliyah, or they should begin retroactively from three verses before. It's written that in some places they customarily call up the scholar for the curses, the Song of the Sea, and the Ten Commandments. Before the rebuke he recites "Musar Hashem beni al tim'as..." and before the Commandments "Rekhev Elokim ribotayim." Also, they call the Levi for the Golden Calf portion and read it quietly. Maharil objected to one who went up for the rebuke—specifically, only the sexton hired for this has no issue. It's written that the forty-two journeys in Parashat Masei should not be interrupted, corresponding to the forty-two letter Name.
text.1_, 427_Siman, 8_Seif Katan: "17th of Tammuz": If one erred and read the haftarah on the first Shabbat from Yoma, the following Shabbat he should read "Divrei Yirmiyahu" and also "Shim'u" since they are adjacent. See section 425. What is written in chumashim "Vayivrach" for Parashat Vayishlach is an error—it belongs to Parashat Vayetzei.
text.1_, 427_Siman, 9_Seif Katan: "Are you not like the children of Kushites": This is also written in Beit Chadash, Magen Avraham, and Agudah, unlike Levush who wrote to read "HaTishpot" even when doubled, since Beit Chadash testified that in all congregations they follow what the Shulchan Aruch wrote.
text.1_, 493_Siman, 0_Seif Katan: I have a difficulty. How can we say on Shavuot that it is "the day of the giving of our Torah"?! Do we not conclude like R. Yose (Shabbat 86b) that the Torah was given on the 7th of Sivan? After all, we do conclude that separation from sexual intercourse [of man and wife, in regard to certain laws of Tumah] requires six half-days, as is written in Yore Deah 196. [R. Yose's opinion -- that the Torah was given on the 7th of Sivan -- is based on a need for husband and wife to separate a full three days. Since the Halakha today requires a 3 days for this particular separation, presumably R. Yose is correct about the date of Revelation.] (And I believe I've seen this question before in some Poseik's writings.)  But in our calendar, Shavuot is always on the 6th of Sivan!     In truth, the Rambam rules in the Laws of Avot haTumah Ch. 5, that we require only three half-days [of separation]. The Kesef Mishna comments there that in the Talmudic text of the Rambam and the Rashba, the Sages only require three half-days, and that the Rambam rules according to them. See there. If so, our custom is in line with the Rambam. What is written in Yoreh Deah, supporting R. Yose, is but stringency [chumra; it is the advised practice, but not the actual letter of the law].       A further difficulty: the Torah was given on the 51st day of their counting! For they left Egypt on the fifth of the week (Wednesday night / Thursday) and the Torah was given on a Shabbat. In this regard, the [book] HaAsarah Maamarot already answered, that it is meant to hint at the Second Day of Yom Tov of the Exiles. In fact, it’s possible that that’s the reason why Moshe added a day of his own accord, but this isn’t the place to discuss it.        ........ It says in the Zohar that the original pious ones would be awake all the night working in Torah.  And already most of those who learn do this.  It's possible to give a reason for this according to its simple understanding, that Israel slept all the night, and the Holy One Blessed be He had to wake them, as the midrash says.  Therefore, we need to fix this.
text.1_, 493_Siman, 4_Seif Katan: Spread out plants: And if Shavuot starts at the end of Shabbos, spread out the plants before Shabbos in accordance with the Maharil.  It is customary to place trees in the the synagogue and in houses, and it seems to me that the reason is so people remember that judgement of fruit trees occurs on Shavuos, and that they should pray for them.
text.1_, 493_Siman, 5_Seif Katan: There are many reasons for eating dairy, I will copy the reason written in the Zohar: the previous seven weeks were in parrallel to the seven clean days a woman counts before immersing in the mikvah, we know that blood becomes milk, this is parallel to the movement from judgement to mercy, and the practice of our fathers is in our hands to fulfill. However, it is important to be careful not to violate any prohibitions (see Yoreh Deah 89)...
text.1_, 550_Siman, 0_Seif Katan: They minimize rejoicing. Meaning they do not rejoice at all, as the Tosafot write in the first chapter of Megillah.
text.1_, 550_Siman, 1_Seif Katan: He should avoid it [a beard-cutting occasion]. Until Rosh Chodesh Elul (Riy"u, and so it appears in the Gemara).
text.1_, 550_Siman, 2_Seif Katan: And the sandak [one who holds the child at a brit]. Apparently this refers specifically to the one who holds the infant on his knees during the circumcision, as stated in Yoreh De'ah 265:11 -- but one who merely brings the child in and out is not included in this. And even though the women likewise customarily wear Shabbos clothing, that is because this is their primary role [in the ceremony]; and certainly on a Shabbos when Tisha B'Av falls out, when it is technically forbidden to wear white garments, it is permitted only to the one who holds the infant -- one does not even change his tallit (Maharil).
text.1_, 550_Siman, 3_Seif Katan: The shirt alone. And this is permitted even if Tisha B'Av falls on Shabbos (Levush); one who is stringent not to change it practices foolish stringency, since [changing] is only on account of perspiration (Matteh Moshe).
text.1_, 550_Siman, 4_Seif Katan: Curtain [parochet]. The same applies to tablecloths and chair coverings (Maharil).
text.1_, 550_Siman, 5_Seif Katan: Shabbos clothing. But new garments are forbidden (Minhagei Chachamim). The Maharil once, when he made a "pidyon ha-ben" [redemption] for his son, wore his Shabbos garments in honor of his son, the bridegroom.
text.1_, 550_Siman, 6_Seif Katan: Of rejoicing. This applies also to business dealings, such as expenses for a wedding canopy, but other ordinary business is permitted as usual (Beit Yosef, Bach). The Maharil wrote that brokers should not carry silverware to broker in the town, since it is [a display of] joy to onlookers; and in a place where the custom is to forbid all business dealings, a formal release [hattarah] is required, as in Yoreh De'ah 214 -- but where the custom is merely to minimize business, no release helps, since there are authorities who hold this way and their ancestors already accepted that view; and in siman 554, end of se'if 2, it implies that one minimizes all business dealings -- see there. The Beit Yosef wrote in the name of the Ran that any construction not needed except for mere convenience is forbidden. If one contracted with a non-Jew for a fixed fee to paint his house, painting is permitted; but if he can appease him for a small sum to wait until after Tisha B'Av, all the better (Maharil). It seems to me that if it is a synagogue, this is a mitzvah of the community and is permitted.
text.1_, 550_Siman, 7_Seif Katan: And for the sake of a mitzvah. For example, one who has no wife and children may build a wedding house (Ran); and the reason people do not customarily marry at all during this period is that it is not an auspicious time (Beit Yosef) -- and therefore the custom is to make new garments for a wedding; but one who has already fulfilled "be fruitful and multiply" is forbidden -- see siman 7.
text.1_, 550_Siman, 8_Seif Katan: And they do not marry. Even without a feast.
text.1_, 550_Siman, 9_Seif Katan: Lest another precede him. For this reason it is permitted to arrange matches (shidduchim); nevertheless it seems to me that making a feast is forbidden, even without dancing and celebrations, and this is not comparable to a brit milah feast which has no joy at all -- unlike here. And it seems to me that even on Shabbos it is forbidden to make [such a feast], since the Gemara states that from Rosh Chodesh until the fast it is forbidden, and it is impossible that there is no Shabbos during that period; however, the custom of eating preserves at the writing of the tenaim (engagement contract) is not called a feast. And it seems to me that dancing and celebrations are forbidden from the 17th of Tammuz onward.
text.1_, 550_Siman, 10_Seif Katan: To cut hair. I have heard that some forbid cutting nails as well, as in mourning; but it seems to me this is not comparable, since this is a matter of private conduct, and regarding private mourning practices, Tisha B'Av is more lenient than [actual] mourning, as the Tosafot write in Perek HaCholetz -- see what I wrote in siman 554:2. And for the honor of Shabbos it is obviously permitted, as stated in se'if 3, and all the more so for the sake of immersion [tevilah].
text.1_, 550_Siman, 11_Seif Katan: And to launder. Because it appears as though one is diverting his mind from the mourning.
text.1_, 550_Siman, 12_Seif Katan: On Tisha B'Av itself. But the Magen Avraham implies that women may wear white, and so it appears in the Bach and Beit Yosef, siman 554, in the name of the Maharik, root 35.
text.1_, 550_Siman, 13_Seif Katan: And likewise for the honor of Shabbos. This implies that for the honor of Shabbos too it is permitted to launder on Thursday, and so it is in the Tur and the Mishnah, and so it appears in se'if 4; and so the Bach writes at the end of this siman, that the custom is to permit it. However, the Darkei Moshe writes: "Bathing we would have permitted on Friday by a kal vachomer from laundering, which is forbidden by law and yet is permitted for the honor of Shabbos, all the more so bathing -- except that the custom is to forbid even bathing" -- implying that laundering, too, has become customarily forbidden; nevertheless, one may be lenient if he has no shirt for Shabbos, and so it appears in the Hagahot Maimoniyot. And through a non-Jew it is obviously permitted. And the Hagahot Ashri writes that haircutting is forbidden even for the honor of Shabbos, and it seems to me the reason is that in any case people are not accustomed to cut hair every single week.
text.1_, 550_Siman, 14_Seif Katan: From Rosh Chodesh onward. Even if he tells [the launderer] to launder it after Tisha B'Av.
text.1_, 550_Siman, 15_Seif Katan: After the fast. And all the more so that meat and wine are permitted, and those who follow the custom of forbidding meat and wine until Shabbos Nachamu are mistaken, and no formal release is needed (Rashal in a responsum). The Bach writes that a release is needed, for it is specifically regarding leaning during the Shema that the Sages held there is no trace of a mitzvah in that leaning, and therefore it is forbidden for one to lean [voluntarily] -- but in all other matters, every person may be stringent for himself, and such people are also forbidden to cut hair and launder until Thursday out of honor for Shabbos -- see what I wrote in siman 63:2. It further seems to me, since Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds in the Gemara that [all such stringencies extend] the entire week [containing Tisha B'Av], the custom follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel; therefore even if the 15th of Av falls on a Friday, meat is forbidden; but if people have the custom to cut hair and launder immediately after the fast, that custom stands, since we cannot obligate them beyond what they have accepted.
text.1_, 550_Siman, 16_Seif Katan: That the custom is to forbid. That is, specifically where [Tisha B'Av] falls on Shabbos and is postponed; but if it falls on Sunday, it is permitted according to all.
text.1_, 550_Siman, 17_Seif Katan: From Thursday. For the honor of Shabbos: if Tisha B'Av falls on Thursday, it is forbidden to launder on Thursday for the sake of Shabbos, even from the afternoon onward (Ran, Beit Yosef, Darkei Moshe, and Levush) -- unlike the Tosafot who are lenient in this matter. The Bach writes that their intent is that on Wednesday, the eve of Tisha B'Av, after midday, it is permitted to launder for the sake of Shabbos, since one cannot wait until Friday out of honor for Shabbos; and the same applies to one traveling far on this Shabbos -- it is permitted to launder for him twice for several Shabbosos, since certainly he cannot wait until after Tisha B'Av; nevertheless it is best to have it done through a non-Jew. But his words are forced and rejected, for it is taught: if it falls on Thursday before [Tisha B'Av], it is forbidden; and if after, it is permitted; if it falls on Friday eve, it is permitted to launder on Thursday for the honor of Shabbos -- and if it were as he says, why does it teach "if it falls on Thursday before, it is forbidden"? It should have taught "if it falls on Thursday, it is permitted to launder on Wednesday for the honor of Shabbos," deriving it a fortiori from the case where it falls on Friday eve, when it is permitted on Thursday, since laundering cannot be done at all on Shabbos -- rather, it must be that when it falls on Thursday it is forbidden to launder on Wednesday, since one can launder on Friday; and furthermore, specifically on Thursday is it permitted since it is recognizable that one is doing so for the sake of Shabbos, unlike on Wednesday -- and so it appears in the Mishnah, second chapter of Taanit. Therefore there is no permission at all to launder on Wednesday, and all the more so for one traveling, that it is forbidden to launder for any other purpose -- know this, for the laundry workers of the House of the Rav were idle [during this period], see Yoreh De'ah 389:1. But if one's thirtieth day [of mourning] falls on the 18th of Tammuz, he may cut his hair, since it is only a custom, and it is a case of "his mourners have come in close succession" (Bach).
text.1_, 550_Siman, 18_Seif Katan: It is forbidden [to launder] for non-Jewish women, etc. Even though by strict law it is permitted, since there is no joy when one launders for others, nevertheless it is forbidden because of appearances, since it is not recognizable that the garments belong to non-Jews (Terumat HaDeshen); and perhaps in private it may be lenient -- see what I wrote in siman 305:11. The same applies where the non-Jews have other [distinctive] clothing, so that it is recognizable that they belong to non-Jews -- it is permitted; see below, in the gloss.
text.1_, 550_Siman, 19_Seif Katan: New garments. It seems to me that the custom is to press garments with a press, in which case they are considered pressed/ironed and forbidden by law; and for this reason the custom is to forbid Shabbos garments [too, if new] -- for even though he has worn them for several Shabbosos, their pressing is still recognizable.
text.1_, 550_Siman, 20_Seif Katan: From Rosh Chodesh onward. The Bach writes that it is forbidden from the 17th of Tammuz onward, since one does not recite Shehecheyanu, as stated in se'if 17; and based on this, what is stated there -- that on Shabbos it is permitted to recite Shehecheyanu -- would imply that it is permitted to wear new garments on the Sabbaths within the Three Weeks; but from Rosh Chodesh onward it is forbidden to wear them even on Shabbos. Alternatively, this refers to one who bought a ready-made garment and recited Shehecheyanu at the time of purchase before the 17th of Tammuz -- in which case it is permitted to wear it during the Three Weeks; but one who bought an unfinished garment and gave it to a craftsman to sew recites the blessing at the time of wearing -- see what I wrote in siman 223:4.
text.1_, 550_Siman, 21_Seif Katan: And new shoes. The same law applies, that it is forbidden to wear them (Agudah, Hagahot Maimoniyot).
text.1_, 550_Siman, 22_Seif Katan: And one should be stringent. Regarding wearing [new garments], the view of the Beit Yosef is to be lenient, since the reason for the prohibition on making [them], as stated in se'if 8, is that the custom is not to warp wool, since the "even shetiyah" [foundation stone] has been nullified, and all mending of garments is included in this, since warping is the beginning of the labor -- so it appears in Terumat HaDeshen and the Beit Yosef. And the Darkei Moshe writes that for this reason even doing it for others is forbidden; and it is implied in Terumat HaDeshen that even doing it to sell in the marketplace is forbidden, but spinning threads is permitted, since it is not included in this. It seems to me that it is permitted to make those called "kronin," which are woven on wood [frames], since this is not a garment -- see se'if 5.
text.1_, 550_Siman, 23_Seif Katan: And the custom is to be lenient in this. This implies that even for a Jew the custom is to be lenient, and this refers to one who gave it to him before Rosh Chodesh; but after Rosh Chodesh it is obviously forbidden to give it.
text.1_, 550_Siman, 24_Seif Katan: To non-Jewish craftsmen. Even though regarding laundering it is forbidden, as stated at the end of se'if 3 -- that is because [laundering] is mentioned in the Gemara as forbidden, unlike new garments; and the reason is that it is not yet his and is not called by his name. And the Hagahot Maimoniyot write that even on Tisha B'Av itself it is permitted to have garments made by a non-Jew for the sake of a wedding -- see what I wrote in se'if 2.
text.1_, 550_Siman, 25_Seif Katan: Not to eat meat. It seems to me that as soon as the congregation has prayed the evening service on Motzaei Shabbos, even though an individual has not yet prayed, he is forbidden in meat and wine; the same applies on Rosh Chodesh for us -- see what I wrote in siman 263 and 291:2, and in the Tur, siman 117, and Yoreh De'ah, end of siman 375; and some abstain from after sunset.
text.1_, 550_Siman, 26_Seif Katan: And vinegar is permitted. See Yoreh De'ah 123, that we are not expert in determining what is called vinegar; nevertheless, here, since it is only a custom, whatever people abstain from drinking due to its sourness is called vinegar, since we follow common usage -- see siman 204:4 and Yoreh De'ah 217. The Bach writes: one who explicitly accepted upon himself not to eat meat from the 17th of Tammuz until Tisha B'Av is forbidden even on Shabbos and requires a formal release. But it seems that anyone who makes a vow with the custom in mind [i.e., intending it to follow the customary pattern] vows [only] with that understanding, and is permitted on Shabbos, as stated in siman 570; however, at the end of the eighth chapter of Nedarim it implies that it is forbidden -- see there in the Ran. Nevertheless it seems to me that whenever one has not expressed it in the language of a formal vow but merely as a simple acceptance, it is permitted on Shabbos -- see siman 518 -- and at a mitzvah feast it is likewise permitted.
text.1_, 550_Siman, 27_Seif Katan: And they put away the knife. See Yoreh De'ah 117, whether it is permitted to slaughter animals [in general, per] se'if 2. They do not slaughter until the 10th of Av; and if Tisha B'Av falls on Thursday, it is permitted to slaughter after midday for the honor of Shabbos (Bach). But the Abudarham writes the reason that from Rosh Chodesh until the fast we decree [against slaughtering] lest one come to eat from it, but on the day of the fast itself this concern does not apply, so it would always be permitted -- see siman 559:10. And it seems to me that in our country, since non-Jews do not eat meat on Friday and Saturday, one would not find buyers for non-kosher meat [from a possibly-treif animal], and therefore it is permitted to slaughter on Wednesday, for otherwise they would refrain and not slaughter at all -- and so it appears from what is stated in se'if 4, and see siman 497 and siman 554:23. And likewise it is written that one who cannot eat dairy foods should eat poultry, since no sacrifice was ever brought from it, and also there is no [special] joy except in the meat of cattle (Bach).
text.1_, 550_Siman, 28_Seif Katan: Are permitted in a cooked dish [containing meat]. Since [the prohibition] is intended to cause distress, and one has indeed become distressed; and furthermore, this is comparable to one who vows against meat, who is permitted a cooked dish, as stated in Yoreh De'ah 216:9. And it seems to me that the fat of meat has the same law as the meat itself, and it is forbidden to eat a cooked dish containing it; and nowadays people are accustomed to forbid even a dish cooked with meat, as the Shach writes in Yoreh De'ah 217:19 regarding vows; and one should not deviate from the custom, since in matters of vows we follow local custom, and furthermore, in a vow people commonly use the language of "eating," in which case by law they would also be forbidden in a cooked dish; and furthermore, the Beit Yosef and Darkei Moshe write to forbid it.
text.1_, 550_Siman, 29_Seif Katan: And salted meat. Even though regarding a "stubborn and rebellious son" it is not considered meat [in that specific context].
text.1_, 550_Siman, 30_Seif Katan: For an infant. This implies that it is permitted to give an infant meat and wine on this Shabbos, since the custom was never to be stringent regarding an infant -- specifically an infant who does not yet know how to mourn for Jerusalem; see siman 343, siman 559:7, and siman 471. And one should not say that it is permitted only for the sake of a mitzvah, for in siman 269 it implies that even for the sake of a mitzvah we do not feed an infant something forbidden -- rather, it must be that there is no prohibition here at all. And in the Hagahot Maimoniyot it is written that the Maharak permitted his young children to eat meat on the eve of [the fast of] Tisha B'Av which fell on Shabbos, after midday -- this implies that he held that for adults it is forbidden but for young children it is permitted; and the reason he wrote "on Shabbos" is that the incident occurred on a Shabbos when [meat] remained for them from the morning meal, as above.
text.1_, 550_Siman, 31_Seif Katan: To drink [the wine of] Havdalah. But if there is no one else, one should recite the blessing without a cup (Maharil) -- see siman 182.
text.1_, 550_Siman, 32_Seif Katan: And the completion of a tractate [siyum]. See Responsa Maharam Mintz, siman 119, and Yesh Sachar, Bava Kamma, chapter 7, se'if 37; and Rabbi Eliezer [in Imrei Shefer], Parshat Metzora, writes that even for the completion of a [single] mitzvah one makes a feast -- see what I wrote in siman 568.
text.1_, 550_Siman, 33_Seif Katan: And an engagement feast. This is difficult, for he wrote in se'if 2 that it is forbidden to make an engagement feast; and the Shach writes in the margin that he found in precise manuscripts of great authorities that "engagement feast" was crossed out; but in the Minhagim it likewise states "engagement feast," and it would be a stretch to erase it from all the texts. The Bach writes that when one has no wife and children it is permitted to make an engagement feast, as stated above in the name of the Ran; however, nowadays the custom is to forbid it even when one has no wife and children. Nevertheless, there is not so much proof from the Ran that a feast is permitted, and moreover, all the halachic authorities imply that by law an engagement feast is forbidden; and it is possible to say that this [leniency] refers to a case where it is not held at the time of the actual engagement, or not in the house of the betrothed, since then there is not so much joy, as stated in siman 546; and even so it is considered a mitzvah feast -- see siman 444, where what is written implies somewhat that it is not considered a mitzvah feast.
text.1_, 550_Siman, 34_Seif Katan: Not to add [to the quorum]. The words of the Maharil: specifically those who attend on account of kinship or friendship [may attend], but those who go merely to drink commit a transgression. And in the Levush he rules as stated in the Minhagim, that from Rosh Chodesh until Tisha B'Av one takes a fixed minimal quorum, and some take ten aside from the relatives connected to the hosts of the feast. And it is written that women connected to this feast are likewise permitted meat and wine -- specifically in a place where women are invited to this feast; but one to whose home [food] is sent is forbidden to eat, as stated in siman 568:2. And it seems to me that specifically those disqualified from testifying [i.e., close relatives] are called "relatives" -- see Yoreh De'ah 374:6 in the gloss; and so it appears in Terumat HaDeshen, siman 291, that one may learn the laws of a wedding feast from those of mourning, and that at the completion of a tractate even one who did not study with them may eat with them on account of kinship or friendship, for Abaye said, "It should be counted to my credit that whenever I saw a Torah scholar who completed a tractate, I made a festive day for all the rabbis" (Responsa Maharam Mintz; Yesh Sachar, end of chapter 7 of Bava Kamma). And it seems to me that one should not follow both leniencies together, but rather either follow the Rema in both his leniency and his stringency, or follow the Levush [consistently]. And [regarding] Tisha B'Av that falls on Shabbos and is postponed -- it does not have the law of "Shabbos on which Tisha B'Av falls" in this regard; on this all agree -- see what I wrote in se'if 4.
text.1_, 550_Siman, 35_Seif Katan: A fixed minimal quorum. And the rest eat dairy food -- see siman 197:3 regarding zimun (the invitation to Grace after Meals).
text.1_, 550_Siman, 36_Seif Katan: On the eve of Tisha B'Av it is permitted. And it seems to me that in any case one should do it before midday, for after that it certainly would not help that afterward one eats a casual meal on the ground, as stated in siman 552:9, since once they are eating meat, one should be more stringent.
text.1_, 550_Siman, 37_Seif Katan: To cut the hair of young children. For young children too are subject to education, whether on account of mourning or on account of distress (Terumat HaDeshen, siman 152); and this requires further study, since in Yoreh De'ah 384 it is ruled that there is no mourning obligation for a minor -- but it seems to me that in communal mourning [as opposed to personal mourning] we are more stringent.
text.1_, 550_Siman, 38_Seif Katan: However, garments, etc. Nevertheless, one should not launder many garments together (Matteh Moshe and Hagahot Maimoniyot); and it seems to me that one should launder privately if one does not launder by the river -- see siman 534.
text.1_, 550_Siman, 39_Seif Katan: Not to bathe. It seems to me that a woman who has given birth is permitted to bathe, as stated in Yoreh De'ah 381:3; and in Berachot 16b the Tosafot write that even on Tisha B'Av itself she is permitted to bathe -- see there; but one should not be lenient in this, since we are not so accustomed to bathing [in general, to know how to gauge this]. When Rosh Chodesh falls on Friday, some have the custom to bathe in honor of Shabbos, and some bathe on the preceding Thursday (Levush and Minhagim); and the Bach writes that one who is accustomed to bathe every Friday and refrains from doing so during this period commits a transgression, and it suffices if he is stringent [only] during the week of Tisha B'Av itself.
text.1_, 550_Siman, 40_Seif Katan: The head with hot water. But it is forbidden to bathe with soap and water and ashes, called "laugh" [lye] (Levush); but as for bathing one's entire body, the universal custom is to forbid it (Darkei Moshe). And one who immerses every Friday for the sake of a mitzvah [ritual immersion] is permitted to immerse on this Shabbos as well (Shelah); nevertheless, one who sometimes omits it because he is occupied with his affairs or because of the cold is forbidden to immerse even now.
text.1_, 550_Siman, 41_Seif Katan: From reciting Shehecheyanu. But on Shabbos it is permitted (Matteh Moshe in the name of Sefer Chassidim and the Levush). And in the writings of the Ari, it is forbidden even on Shabbos. And it seems to me that if the 17th of Tammuz falls on Shabbos and is postponed [to Sunday], it is permitted according to all -- see se'if 4. And the reason for the prohibition, it seems to me, is that since this is a time of misfortune, one should not recite Shehecheyanu for such a time; but the reason is not on account of mourning, for we do not find that a mourner is forbidden to recite Shehecheyanu.
text.1_, 550_Siman, 42_Seif Katan: And should not delay the mitzvah [or blessing]. Or the blessing (Maharil); and even though when one sees a new fruit the blessing is [technically] delayed, nevertheless, since the custom is to wait until the time of eating, this is not called delaying the blessing, see siman 225.
text.1_, 550_Siman, 43_Seif Katan: Lest it not be found. And according to the view of those who permit it on Shabbos, one must say that even on Shabbos it is not available, and if one takes it during the week and saves it for Shabbos it would spoil -- such as small cherries.
text.1_, 550_Siman, 44_Seif Katan: From the 4th until the 9th. In Eichah Rabbati it states from the end of the 4th until the beginning of the 9th; and in Bamidbar Rabbati it states from the beginning of the 4th until the end of the 9th; and in the Kavvanot of the Ari it is written that one should mourn during those days after midday and weep for about half an hour.
text.1_, 560_Siman, 1_Seif Katan: Rambam rules (Beit HaBechira, chapter 6) that the holiness of the courtyard and of Jerusalem is eternal. See also Yevamot 82 in Tosafot and the Raavad disagree in various places. In the Mishnah (Mishnah maaser Sheni 1:5) it says that if there is no mikdash it [maaser] should be left to rot. If this is so, there is no holiness even for he that enters there, and there is no [penalty of] karet. [...] The words of the Rambam are correct that one who enters the place of the mikdash is liable for karet because we are all tamei met.
text.1_, 575_Siman, 2_Seif Katan: "For the ill" - And this law also applies, that when varicella (chickenpox) blossoms in babies and they die, one should decree a fast, and the Gaon Rabbi Moshe already wrote a prayer for this, and the Shla"h wrote that that one should take one's children out from the city during a time like this, and if one does not do this, they are obligated with their lives (i.e. it involves a serious punishment).
text.1_, 638_Siman, 7_Seif Katan: A Man and His Wife. Such is apparent from the beginning of Arakhin [Arakhin 3b] where they say that priests are exempt from the Sukkah during the Avodah, see there. And this requires further study, for in Sukkah 28b: Since you might have thought, sit such as you dwell, since one dwells husband and wife, so too Sukkah must be husband and wife, so you have learned that women are exempt. And it should be said, that anyway the husband is not obligated in the Sukkah but where he can dwell there with his wife, and if not, he is Mitzta'er (discomforted) and is exempt from sleeping there, and such wrote the Shela"h, see there. But anyway, this is still difficult, since if he made the Sukkah in a place where he cannot sleep, he has not fulfilled his obligation [when he sits in it], as is written in the Rem"a in Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayyim 640:14, and if so, if he does not have a Sukkah which is isolated [so that he can sleep there with his wife modestly] he has not fulfilled his obligation at all [even when he eats therein], and another difficulty is that in the Gemara we say that "all of Israel are fit to sit in one Sukkah", see there. And it must be said that since he can sleep there alone, the Sukkah is valid, for it is a residence, but he is anyway exempt, for he is considered discomforted.
text.1_, 669_Siman, 0_Seif Katan: It is the practice for the poor to circulate to [people's] doors (to ask for charity) on Chanukkah. And in the book, Chanukkat HaBayit, [its author] wrote a reason for this. Women: Specifically women, since the miracle happened through them (Mateh Moshe).
